summary:
The Republic of Kosovo's constitution was adopted on 9 April 2008 and entered into force on 15 June 2008. It guarantees equality before the law, treats human dignity as inviolable, and prohibits discrimination on grounds including gender and sexual orientation. The Anti-Discrimination Law was amended on 26 May 2015 and took effect in July 2015, adding gender identity to the protected grounds. It covers employment, membership of organisations, education, provision of goods and services, social security, and access to housing, and defines discrimination to include direct and indirect discrimination, harassment, victimisation and segregation. Outright International's March 2026 overview records that implementation of both the constitutional prohibition and the 2015 statute remains inconsistent in practice, so the protections a visitor can cite are broader than what is reliably delivered.

The Criminal Code in force from April 2019 provides additional penalties for hate crimes motivated by the victim's gender identity, alongside the equivalent provision covering sexual orientation.

Sexual conduct between people of the same sex has been lawful in Kosovo since independence in 2008. The 2004 UNMIK regulation set the age of consent at 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation and made all sexual offences gender-neutral.

Legal gender recognition has no administrative procedure in Kosovo and runs through the courts. Kosovo's Civil Registration Agency rejected Blert Morina's application for a name and gender-marker change on his identity documents, and constitutional review of the matter was requested in July 2018. In December 2019 the Basic Court of Pristina ruled in his favour, holding that his name and sex marker could be changed without evidence of surgical intervention or any other medical change. The Ministry of Justice and the Civil Registration Agency have stated that the judgment will not be treated as precedent and that other transgender people will have to go through a similar court procedure. No source in the inventory identifies a standing administrative route available to applicants generally, and the only documented successful route is individual litigation.

Partnership recognition has not been extended. Article 14 of the Law on Family defines marriage as a legally registered community of two persons of different sexes. The Assembly rejected a civil-partnership provision in the new Civil Code on 16 March 2022, with only 28 of 120 MPs voting in favour. Reuters reported in May 2024 that the debate over same-sex unions was proceeding amid fierce opposition in the Muslim-majority country. Prime Minister Albin Kurti announced an intent to legalise same-sex unions on 25 April 2024. As of February 2026 Parliament had still failed to adopt the new Civil Code amid opposition that included the ruling party. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect no legal recognition of that partnership, in the form of either marriage or civil union.

Enforcement and reporting of anti-LGBTQ violence are weak. LGBTQ people in Kosovo tend to avoid reporting discrimination or abuse to the police. Ten bias-motivated crimes against LGBTQ people were reported to the authorities in 2019, with a further 13 reported only to LGBTQ organisations. In February 2019 the authorities initiated a case against a Ministry of Justice official who had called for LGBTQ people to be beheaded, and police took him into custody.

Public organising in the capital is established and visible. The first pride parade in Pristina was held in May 2016, and Pride Week has been held annually since 2017; the third annual parade was accompanied by a week of exhibitions, parties, conferences and discussions organised by the Center for Equality and Liberty, under a slogan framed as both an appeal for tolerance and an invitation to join the parade. The October 2019 march from Skanderbeg Square down Mother Teresa Boulevard to Zahir Pajaziti Square was held without incident but under multiple threats; anonymous threats warning people not to attend were especially pronounced in 2017. Government engagement has included a late-2013 parliamentary bill creating a coordinating group for the LGBTQ community and a 17 May 2014 march against homophobia by politicians and diplomats, welcomed by the European Union office and the government, with a large LGBTQ flag covering the front of the government building that night.

Survey evidence documents widespread societal hostility, but not in terms specific to transgender people. A 2015 National Democratic Institute survey found that 81 per cent of LGBTQ Kosovars said they had been subjected to psychological abuse and that 29 per cent reported being victims of physical violence; the same body found that over 97 per cent of respondents would not accept a child who came out as lesbian or gay. These figures cover LGBTQ respondents generally, are not disaggregated for transgender people, date from 2015, and are given without a general-population comparison.
tangentialFactors:
Regional litigation has shaped the domestic argument over gender-marker change. In January 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled in X v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia that a surgical requirement for changing a gender marker violates the right to private life. Applicants in Kosovo, including Blert Morina while his own constitutional case was pending, followed that ruling closely.

The constitutional status of relationship recognition is contested even without legislation. In 2014 the President of the Constitutional Court said Kosovo de jure allows same-sex marriage, and Article 144(3) of the constitution requires Constitutional Court approval of amendments in order to ensure they do not infringe previously guaranteed civil rights. Analysis of the Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language has argued that it would open the way for gay marriage. During Pride week the Prime Minister said he would do his utmost to get the Civil Code adopted, and a Justice Ministry working group was drafting a bill.

Two adjacent rules sit outside the trans-specific framework but bear on services. A 2018 Blood Donation Week guideline bars people who have intimate relationships with the same sex from donating blood. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people are permitted to serve openly in the military, though they may face discrimination from peers.

Advocacy reporting describes an environment of intolerance around the Civil Code debates. CSGD's 2022 annual report found intolerance and hatred, with hate speech by politicians common during those debates, and an artist received death threats over a painting.
localsOnly:
The Center for Social Emancipation (CSGD) provides LGBTQI+ people in Kosovo with free confidential legal aid and psychological support, in person and online through its app, along with tailored reproductive and sexual health services that include support navigating hormonal procedures for transgender people in cooperation with the ministry, and free HIV testing. Free PrEP HIV-prevention treatment has been available at the QKUK Infectious Disease Clinic since 12 June 2024, following CSGD's advocacy.

Discrimination and stigmatisation against the LGBTQ+ community remain widespread among the general population even though they are outlawed. The Center for Social Emancipation describes gay life in Kosovo as underground and mostly secretive, with one gay bar in the capital.

Relationship-recognition legislation is still in drafting. A Justice Ministry working group was preparing a bill, and the Prime Minister committed during Pride week to pressing for adoption of the Civil Code; Parliament had not adopted it as of February 2026.
outOfScopeNotes:
The availability of legal gender recognition as a general rule is unresolved across the sources. One overview states that transgender people in Kosovo are not allowed to legally change their gender even if they have undergone sex reassignment surgery. That sits against the December 2019 Basic Court of Pristina judgment, which recognised a change of name and sex marker without surgical or medical evidence for the individual applicant, and against the model of case-by-case litigation described by the Ministry of Justice and the Civil Registration Agency. No source in this inventory records a later case testing whether the courts will follow the 2019 judgment, and none identifies an administrative procedure.

Data on violence and abuse are not disaggregated for transgender people. The 2015 National Democratic Institute figures cover LGBTQ respondents as a whole and are a decade old; the source provides no general-population rate against which to read them.

The hate-crime figures for 2019 are raw counts of reports, not incidence: 10 reports to authorities and 13 to LGBTQ organisations. Advocacy sources describe reluctance among LGBTQ people to report to police, so the recorded numbers understate what occurs and cannot be used to compare Kosovo's risk level with any other jurisdiction.

Whether the Civil Code will be adopted, and whether it will retain gender-neutral marriage language or a civil-union provision, was unresolved as of February 2026.
